Short term this may have helped with "paid" reviews (which were a few hundred games max out of tens of thousands), but long term this is going to do nothing but hurt the review process on Steam. If someone really wants to pay people for reviews, it's still as simple as sending someone money through Paypal to buy the game for "feedback" with an understanding that a positive review is expected. It might be slightly more expensive, but the results are the same as giving out codes except that Steam gets 30% of the game price in the process and people who got a key somehow can't leave honest reviews to balance it out. If they're just after positive reviews, marking the game down to virtually nothing always generates good reviews anyway, no free keys or payment required. All this does is make it so developers that are on the up and up are put at a disadvantage while not really doing anything about review manipulation.

Honestly, this is a cop out by Steam to keep from having to actually police their store. When you have shit like Infestation: Survivor Stories (aka WarZ) and Digital Homicide's selection of stolen asset flips, the system is clearly abusable. Game quality is subjective, but a couple of high-profile game delistings for paid reviews, which are clearly in the wrong, and it'd never be a problem again. At the very least count the key reviews partially into the score, possibly discounting reviews when there are a large number of positive reviews from keys in a short amount of time. Or Make the default include key reviews and be able to exclude them if you want. There are a number of ways that Valve could've done this, but once again their laziness and apathy shined through and they took the path of least effort needed.
